w: Dr. Kaur taught this session in class on Oct 29, with her slides. Her question: should people who have had gum disease (periodontitis) get implants? Her answer: yes, once the gum disease is treated, under control, and the patient keeps up with care. Along the way she showed how to tell a healthy implant from a sick one, the same way you already tell healthy gums from gingivitis and periodontitis. Success versus survival An implant that survives is just still there and has a crown on it. It can still have problems: inflamed gums around it, bone loss, a broken or loose part, pain or gum shrinking back. A successful implant has no problems at all. Research papers use both words, so check which one they mean. The success rules on her slide are Albrektsson's from 1986: the implant doesn't move, there's no dark ring around it on the X-ray, there's no pain, infection, numbness or nerve trouble, and it has lost 1.5 mm of bone or less after its first year of use. In class she added: after that first year, no more than 0.2 mm a year. A dark area at the tip of the implant is called retrograde peri-implantitis. Healthy, inflamed, diseased: the 2017 names In 2017 an expert workshop gave names to the states around an implant: peri-implant health, peri-implant mucositis (gum inflammation only), peri-implantitis (inflammation plus bone loss), and soft and hard tissue deficiency (gum and bone both lost). Health. No redness or swelling, no bleeding or pus when you probe gently, no deeper reading than at earlier visits, and no bone loss beyond the normal settling after the implant goes in. There's no 3 mm limit: a healthy implant can probe deeper than 3 mm, depending on how deep it was placed, how tall the connecting piece is, and how thick the gum is. Probing implants accurately is hard, even with a plastic probe. So you always compare an implant with its own starting records, and you have to take those records at the start. Normal settling. Once an implant starts chewing, the bone at its top reshapes. In class she said about 2 mm, and it levels off within about the first year. That's normal. Any bone loss past that is disease. Peri-implant mucositis is like gingivitis around an implant: redness and swelling, heavy bleeding (a line or a drop) and/or pus when probed gently, a deeper reading than at the start, but no extra bone loss. The pocket is deeper only because the gum is swollen. It can be reversed, so treat it, don't just watch it. A pocket reading goes up for only three reasons: a measuring mistake, swollen gum, or real bone loss. Pus means the disease is active right now, at a tooth or an implant, and you have to do something that day: clean the area, and sometimes put an antibiotic into a deep pocket (Session 8). Peri-implantitis has all the signs of inflammation plus bone loss beyond the normal settling. When you hear the word, picture real bone loss. The official definition: a disease caused by plaque, with inflamed gums around the implant followed by ongoing bone loss. That's why you stop it while it's still only mucositis. It's hard to fix. In theory only bone has to grow back (implants have no ligament or root surface to rebuild). The trouble is the implant surface: it's made rough on purpose so bone grabs it, and plaque grabs it too. Nothing cleans it better than anything else: salt water, chlorhexidine, citric acid, EDTA and lasers all work about the same. The bone holes around implants are usually not the narrow, deep shape that heals best, and the disease often comes back. A site with an 8-9 mm pocket, pus and bone loss but with bone still standing on the sides and the tongue side can still be treated: open it, clean it, add a growth factor or bone graft, cover it with a membrane and close. Soft and hard tissue deficiency means the gum is lost along with the bone under it. Thin gum shrinks back faster than thick gum. Ailing, failing, failed (Meffert 1992) Ailing: bone was lost but the loss has stopped; no inflammation and the implant doesn't move. Watch it and record it at every visit. Failing: bone loss is still going on and the gum is inflamed, but the implant doesn't move; what to do depends on the case. Failed: bone loss, the implant moves, and it no longer works. A moving implant has lost its bond to the bone (osseointegration), which can never be undone, so it has to come out. First make sure it's the implant itself that moves, not just the connector or the crown. Peri-implantitis rarely makes an implant loose, even with two-thirds of its bone gone. An implant with bone loss that bad still counts as failed if it has no future. What causes it Many things add up, but the cause is plaque bacteria, and they're the same bad bacteria as in gum disease. Risk factors come from the patient, the surgery and implant, the gum, and the crown. Risk factors for mucositis: smoking (now or in the past), past gum disease, active gum disease, thin gum, and obesity or metabolic syndrome. Risk factors for peri-implantitis: smoking, past or active gum disease, obesity or metabolic syndrome, an implant in the wrong position, poorly controlled diabetes, too little bone width, and depression or antidepressants. Poor brushing and flossing raised the odds about 14 times in one study. Germs. The bacteria in the mouth before the implant goes in decide which bacteria live around it. Around healthy implants, the bacteria look like those under healthy gums. Genes matter too. A coating from saliva (the pellicle) forms on an implant within 30 minutes of it being exposed. The first settlers are harmless round and rod-shaped bacteria (gram-positive, including Actinomyces); later the gum-disease bacteria move in (P. gingivalis, P. intermedia). Why it matters how the teeth were lost Someone who lost teeth to gum disease is a susceptible host, with a higher risk of implant disease, even with no teeth left. Gum-disease bacteria can hang around a year or more after the teeth are pulled. So untreated gum disease rules implants out, but someone whose gum disease is treated and kept under control can have implants, with closer check-ups. Do things in order: deep cleaning first; pull hopeless teeth but don't put implants in yet; let things heal and teach good home care; re-check; do any gum surgery; and only then plan implants. Check the risks again at each step. One or two surgeries. In a two-stage implant, a cap goes on and the gum is closed over it; about 3-4 months later it's uncovered, a healing post that sticks through the gum goes on, and 2-3 weeks later the impression is taken. In a single-stage implant the healing post goes on the same day. The #31 case. A 41-year-old man with untreated gum disease got an implant at #31 with a bone graft next to #30, then never came back for care. Two years later his only complaint was food getting stuck. Gum and bone were both gone around #31. The implant was unscrewed and removed, #30 was also pulled, the bone was rebuilt in height, and two new implants went in. A gentler option would have been a root canal on #30 and removing only its bad root. A 2006 European consensus found more peri-implantitis and more bone loss in people who lost teeth to gum disease, and a 10-year study found that people with gum disease lost more implants. The challenges Gum loss: missing papillae, black triangles and less firm (keratinized) gum, worse with thin gum. Both how much firm gum there is and how thick it is matter, most of all in the smile zone. Bone loss: an implant in short bone carries a long crown, and that can break the implant. Growing bone wider is much easier than growing it taller. A sinus lift is the easy kind of taller, since the bone grows up into the sinus. In one patient missing #1-7, the bone was too short, the front implants were lost, and he ended up with a removable denture on the remaining implants. Ways to add bone: grafting a socket, building up the ridge, sinus lifts; moving the nerve or using short implants; and distraction osteogenesis (slowly stretching bone to make it taller). Checking risk at every step Check the risks before the implant goes in, while it heals into the bone, at every maintenance visit, and after an implant is removed. Anything that raises the risk of gum disease also raises the risk of implant failure. Smoking hurts three ways. Germs: smokers carry nastier bacteria that are harder to clear (A. actinomycetemcomitans, P. gingivalis, B. forsythus), and smoke lowers oxygen, which those bacteria like. Immune system: white cells move and eat bacteria poorly, there are fewer helper T cells and B cells, and more inflammatory signals (IL-6, TNF-alpha) and tissue-breaking collagenase. Healing: nicotine slows new blood vessel growth. In one study of 2,194 implants, 11.3% failed in smokers vs 4.76% in nonsmokers; heavier smokers do worse (the more you smoke, the worse it gets); and peri-implantitis hit 23.5% of smokers vs 16.5% of nonsmokers. Risk starts below a pack a day. Vaping hasn't been studied long; it may not squeeze blood vessels the way smoke does, but it still weakens the immune response. Diabetes. How long someone has had diabetes doesn't matter if it's well controlled. Poorly controlled diabetes rules implants out. Control is measured with HbA1c, which shows the last 3-4 months because that's how long red blood cells live. (Outside the lecture: UAB's clinic says no to implants at an HbA1c of 8 or higher.) From the exam-review guide: some people carry IL-1 gene variants that make them overreact to bacteria, and that gene plus smoking raises peri-implantitis risk more than the two would add up to. Check-ups: probing, bleeding and X-rays Implants are checked with plastic implant probes and cleaned with implant scalers. At each visit look at: bleeding when probed lightly (about 0.25 N), the gum, pus, pocket depth, pain, movement and bone loss on X-ray. Bleeding can come from probing too hard or at the wrong angle, or from inflamed gum. No bleeding is a good sign that the implant is stable. Bleeding means inflammation but doesn't prove the disease is getting worse. A little slow bleeding may be nothing; heavy bleeding that fills the pocket is a warning. Follow it over time: a site that bled at all 4 visits had a 30% chance of losing attachment, 3 of 4 visits 14%, 2 of 4 6%, 1 of 4 3%, and never 1.5%. X-rays are taken when the implant goes in, before it's uncovered (or before the crown work if it's one surgery), at the final impression, when the final connector goes on, and when the final crown goes on (the starting X-ray); then every 6 months in the first year, then once a year. Take an extra one only when probing shows a change (deeper pocket, bleeding, pus): X-rays confirm what you found, they're not for fishing. Bottom line Checking and controlling risk is part of implant care. Tell patients with past gum disease that their risk is higher. Treat gum disease before placing implants. Good home care and regular check-ups decide the outcome, so make the patient your partner. A patient whose gum disease is treated, stable and who keeps up with care can have implants.
